note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in MT.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Giant Springs Road
byways.where: Giant Springs Road, Great Falls, from River Drive to the railroad tracks (MDT routes U-5221 and part of L-7-1041), about 2.2 mi, Cascade County

facts.fact: On May 26, 2011 the Transportation Commission designated Giant Springs Road from River Drive to the railroad tracks, U-5221 (1.388 mi) and part of L-7-1041 (0.81 mi), as a Montana Scenic-Historic Byway; the segment was shortened to avoid private land at the end.

Testimony at the designation described the road as passing Giant Springs State Park, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center and the River's Edge Trail, with the city owning the western part and Cascade County the eastern.
Giant Springs, first recorded by Lewis and Clark in 1805, produces over 156 million gallons a day and spills into the Roe River, once listed by Guinness as the world's shortest river.
The spring water holds a constant 54 °F.

byways.review: Not in the catalog. Official page is the state park's, since the road has none of its own. MDT said a corridor management plan was needed before signing; no evidence one was finished.

byways.name: Lake Koocanusa
byways.designation: Montana Scenic-Historic Byway (designated May 26, 2011); also National Forest Scenic Byway (1992)
byways.where: MT 37 (MDT route P-33) from MP 16 to MP 58, along the east shore of Lake Koocanusa between Libby and Eureka, Lincoln County

facts.fact: The Commission designated MT 37 from MP 16 to MP 58, about 42 miles almost entirely bordered by Forest Service land, as a Montana Scenic-Historic Byway on May 26, 2011, with the Forest Service as sponsor and a condition that MDT consult the Tribe on the corridor plan.
The Forest Service byway, created in 1992, runs 67 miles on MT 37 from Libby to Eureka, with a paved side loop (Forest Road 228) on the lake's west side closed in winter.
Lake Koocanusa formed behind Libby Dam, completed in 1974, and reaches 90 miles north into British Columbia; its name joins Kootenai, Canada and USA.
The lake fills a narrow fjord-like gorge between the Purcell and Salish mountains, and bighorn sheep are often seen on rock ledges along the road.

byways.review: The state designation covers only MP 16 to 58 (about 42 mi). The catalog line (113 mi) is the full 1992 Forest Service byway including the FR 228 west-side loop. The catalog's designation field wrongly says 'Alaska State Scenic Byway'.

byways.name: Beartooth Highway
byways.designation: All-American Road (2002); also National Forest Scenic Byway (1989)
byways.where: US 212 from Red Lodge over Beartooth Pass (in Wyoming) to Cooke City and Yellowstone's Northeast Entrance, Carbon and Park counties

facts.fact: Construction began in 1932 and the highway was completed on June 14, 1936.
South of Red Lodge the road climbs switchbacks to the Wyoming line, crests Beartooth Pass at 10,947 feet and re-enters Montana just before Cooke City.
Snow usually lingers at higher elevations until early to mid-July, and MDT closes the highway every winter.
The 68-mile route was designated an All-American Road in 2002.

byways.review: Not a member of the Montana state program; the 2011 Commission minutes call it the only Montana road designated at the national level. Also listed in the Wyoming chapter.

byways.name: Kings Hill Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 89 for 71 mi from US 12 near White Sulphur Springs north to US 87 near Armington, via Neihart; Meagher and Cascade counties

facts.fact: The 71-mile byway follows US 89 from US 12 through the Little Belt Mountains and the Lewis and Clark National Forest, through Neihart and Monarch, to US 87.
Kings Hill Pass stands at 7,393 feet.
Neihart grew from an 1881 silver strike, and about $16 million in silver came out of the area between 1882 and 1929.
Showdown Ski Area lies just south of Kings Hill Pass.

byways.review: Not a state byway: at the May 2011 Commission meeting MDT staff said Kings Hill is a Forest Service byway, not part of the state program.

byways.name: Pioneer Mountains Scenic Byway
byways.where: Wise River Road from MT 43 at Wise River south to MT 278, Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest, Beaverhead County

facts.fact: The byway runs the length of the Pioneer Mountains, with granite peaks over 10,000 feet to the east, and crosses a 7,800-foot divide between the Wise River and Grasshopper Creek.
Travelers can visit the ghost town of Coolidge and the abandoned Elkhorn silver mine, and soak at Elkhorn Hot Springs, about 100 degrees.
The paved Wise River Road divides the range into the East and West Pioneers.

byways.name: St. Regis-Paradise Scenic Byway
byways.where: MT 135, 21.5 mi from I-90 at St. Regis to MT 200 near Paradise, Mineral and Sanders counties

facts.fact: MT 135 runs 21.5 miles from I-90 at St. Regis along the Clark Fork through the Lolo National Forest to MT 200 near Paradise, crossing the river near its midpoint with a rail line alongside.
A toll ferry once crossed the Clark Fork on the old secondary route here.
The byway passes from open, rolling flats to steep canyon walls.
MDT records the St. Regis-Paradise Scenic Byway on MT 135 as a 1992 federal designation.

byways.review: No Forest Service page found; the URL is Visit Montana's Clark Fork Scenic Drive, which includes the byway.

byways.name: Big Sheep Creek Back Country Byway
byways.where: Big Sheep Creek Road and Medicine Lodge Road, about 50 mi from I-15 at Dell to MT 324 near Grant, Beaverhead County

facts.fact: The gravel byway leaves I-15 at Dell, runs through Big Sheep Canyon in the Tendoy Mountains and north into the Medicine Lodge valley, and can also be reached from MT 324.
There are no services or potable water on the route; Deadwood Campground lies about 10 miles in.
From the road you can look down into the clear, deep pools of spring-fed Big Sheep Creek and see many trout.

byways.review: BLM gives 1989 as the designation year; MDT's layer says 1990.

byways.name: Big Sky Back Country Byway
byways.where: MT 253, MT 200 and MT 13, 105 mi from Terry via Circle to Wolf Point; Prairie, McCone and Roosevelt counties

facts.fact: The 105-mile byway runs from Terry north on MT 253, MT 200 and MT 13 through Circle to Wolf Point on the Missouri, and is now paved all the way.
The route follows part of the Regina-Yellowstone Trail, which Canadian tourists once used to reach Yellowstone, past dry-land farms, prairie, scoria buttes and badlands.
The northern end looks onto the historic Lewis and Clark Bridge over the Missouri.

byways.name: Garnet Back Country Byway
byways.where: Garnet Range Road, 12 mi from MT 200 near Potomac (about 30 mi east of Missoula) to Garnet Ghost Town, Granite County

facts.fact: The 12-mile byway climbs 2,000 feet through the Garnet Range to Garnet Ghost Town, where 30 preserved buildings look much as they did in 1895.
About a thousand people lived in Garnet in the 1890s; the town was largely abandoned about 20 years later when the gold ran out.
The BLM marks and grooms the route for snowmobiles from January 1 to April 30.

byways.name: Missouri Breaks Back Country Byway
byways.where: Back roads from MT 236 at Winifred north and east to US 191 near the Fred Robinson Bridge, Fergus and Phillips counties

facts.fact: Lewis and Clark called this country 'the Deserts of America', and fur traders named this stretch of the Missouri Mauvaises Terres, the bad lands.
The byway overlooks the Upper Missouri National Wild and Scenic River, designated in 1976, and from Winifred to Deweese Ridge closely follows the Nez Perce National Historic Trail.
The route runs from MT 236 in Winifred to Knox Ridge Road and US 191 near the Fred Robinson Bridge, through the Upper Missouri River Breaks National Monument.

byways.review: BLM's byway page (blm.gov/visit/missouri-breaks-back-country-byway) now returns 'not published or has moved'; URL is Visit Montana's listing. Length differs: Wikipedia 80 mi, catalog 60 mi.

issues: MDT's program page lists no routes. The only designations found are Giant Springs Road and Lake Koocanusa (MT 37 MP 16 to 58), both approved May 26, 2011; Commission minutes of Nov 7, 2024 confirm these two are the only ones and that 2011 was the last time the council acted.

The registry note's secondary sources calling Kings Hill, Pioneer Mountains and Clark Fork state byways are wrong: in the 2011 minutes MDT staff said Kings Hill is a Forest Service byway, not a state one. They are listed here under the Forest Service.

Catalog lake-koocanusa-scenic-byway-2135 has designation 'Alaska State Scenic Byway', which is an error; it should read Montana Scenic-Historic Byway (MP 16 to 58 only) plus National Forest Scenic Byway. The catalog line (113 mi) is the full Forest Service byway, much longer than the 42-mile state segment.

Giant Springs Road is not in the catalog. Its gisWhere on the MDT Route Name layer draws about 2.73 mi, roughly half a mile longer than the designated 2.2 mi (it continues past the railroad tracks toward 67th St N).
The 2011 designations were to be signed only once corridor management plans were done; no evidence found that either plan was completed or that the routes are signed.
In December 2024 the MDT director said a bill was being drafted so the advisory council would no longer be required; whether it passed in the 2025 session was not checked.

Pintler Veterans' Memorial Scenic Highway (MT 1, Anaconda to Drummond, MCA 60-1-219, 2011) is a legislative memorial name, not a state byway; the Commission found the route ineligible because of private land. Not in the catalog.
BLM's Missouri Breaks Back Country Byway page no longer exists. Big Sheep Creek designation year is 1989 (BLM) vs 1990 (MDT layer).
Going-to-the-Sun Road was expected to apply for state designation in 2012 or 2013 (Oct 2010 council minutes) but was never designated; it stays a classic drive.
